I served in the mounted forces of the Haven of Umbar, patrolling the borders and striking fast against the navy of Gondor's raiding parties. My horsemanship was unmatched among the Corsairs of Umbar.
During a raid, my commander ordered us to trample fleeing civilians - they might be enemy sympathizers, he said. I refused and was court-martialed for disobedience.
Now I ride alone, my lance for hire to those who fight with honor. The open road suits me better than garrison duty ever did.
A rider who values life over orders has true courage.
Disobedience in battle can cost more lives than it saves.
Give me a mount and a cause worth riding for.
A galley master from the Haven of Umbar, seeking purpose and adventure.
An arrow loosed at the right moment can change history...

I was the finest marksman in the Haven of Umbar, able to split an arrow at two hundred paces. I served as the Corsair Lords's personal guard archer, watching over the Corsairs of Umbar from the highest vantage points.
But I witnessed my captain murder a prisoner in cold blood and reported it. The captain was connected to powerful families, and suddenly I was the one accused of crimes I didn't commit.
I escaped before they could silence me permanently. Now I offer my bow to those who still believe in justice. Every arrow I loose carries the memory of that murdered prisoner.
Justice is worth fighting for, even at great cost.
The dead don't care about justice.
My bow is steady and my aim is true. Will you have me?
A crossbow ace from the Haven of Umbar, seeking purpose and adventure.
The steppe breeds hard riders, and the Ezarkia hardest of all. Ask, and I will tell you how I came to ride alone.

I led the raiding lances of clan Ezarkia, foremost of the nine tribes of Shaghâna. From the saddle I broke caravans and border forts alike, and brought back more plunder than any rider of my year. The Taskral himself knew my name.

Then a blood-feud took my cousins, and the elders judged that I had spilled kin to settle it. Whether the charge was true or merely convenient, the oath that bound me to the clan was cut. A rider without a clan is a dead man on the steppe, so I rode west before they could make it so.

Now my lance answers to coin, and to whoever rides against true enemies. The Taskral musters the tribes for the Dark Lord's war, and there will be plunder enough for any who can take it. I mean to be among them, on my own terms this time.
A raider cast out by his own blood, but a useful one.
Ruthless on the steppe, ruthless in my service. I can use that.
Give me a horse beneath me and an enemy ahead, and you will not find a harder lance for hire.
An exiled raid-leader of clan Ezarkia, riding for whoever pays and fights.
Talk is cheap, and I do not give it away. But for you I will make an exception.

I kept the tribute-ledgers of clan Kûmaraknis. Every head of cattle, every weight of silver the tribes owed the Taskral passed under my reckoning. I knew to the grain what each fortress could pay, and what it tried to hide.

A man who counts coin all day learns where coin goes missing, and learns the trick of it himself. When the discrepancy was found, the elders wanted my hands. I left with the contents of one strongbox and the clothes I stood in.

Coin still loves me and I still love it. I can supply a war-band cheaper than any quartermaster you will hire, skim a little for myself, and you will never feel the loss. The steppe taught me that a full belly beats a clean conscience.
A thief who keeps good books is still worth his wage.
He robbed his own clan. He would rob me the moment it paid.
Put me over your stores and your purse, and both will go further than you think.
A disgraced tribute-keeper of clan Kûmaraknis, selling his reckoning to the highest bidder.
You want the truth of it? Few do. But I have never learned to lie comfortably, so listen.
I rode in the war-host of clan Taiymâkä and swore the blood-oath young, as we all do. I held it more dearly than most. To me an oath was the only thing on the steppe a man truly owns.

My captain ordered the lances to ride down a column of unarmed pilgrims on the Taskral's road, to make an example. I would not, and I said why before the whole host. They named me oath-breaker for breaking faith with my captain, never mind the faith I kept with the helpless.

So I keep my own counsel and my own oath now, and sell my sword only to those who will not make me ashamed to draw it. There is a war coming that will swallow honest men whole. I would rather choose where I spend mine.
An honest blade is rare. I will take it gladly.
A man too proud to follow orders is a danger in a fight.
My oath is yours so long as you keep faith. Break it, and I am gone.
An oath-keeper of clan Taiymâkä, exiled for refusing a captain's cruel command.
I have set more bones than I have broken, which on the steppe is a strange thing to say. Sit, and I will tell you why I wander.

I was bonesetter and herb-healer to clan Zayaknûri, riding behind the war-host to mend what battle broke. The old women taught me which steppe roots draw fever and which seal a wound, and for many years my hands saved more riders than any lance took.

But the raids grew crueler as the Taskral bent the tribes to the Dark Lord's purpose. I was made to walk the fields after and finish the enemy wounded rather than tend them. The third time, I could not, and a healer who will not kill is no use to a war-clan.

Now I go where the hurt are and ask few questions about which banner they bleed under. Hard times are coming for the steppe, and afterward there will be more wounded than healers to meet them. I would be one of the healers.
A healer is worth ten swords on a long campaign.
A man who flinches from killing will flinch when I need him.
Keep me near your wounded and I will keep your riders in the saddle longer than you would believe.
A steppe bonesetter of clan Zayaknûri, who left rather than slay the helpless.
Ha, you have the look of someone with a story of their own. Trade me yours and I will give you mine. No? Then take mine for free.

I was the best horse-thief clan Selarkes ever raised, which is no small boast among a people who measure a man by the mounts he can take. I could walk into a rival fortress's pens and walk out with their finest stallion, and they would not wake until I was a league gone.

Trouble is, I never could keep what I took. A good horse to a friend in need, silver to a hungry family, it all ran through my fingers. When I lifted mounts from a clan the Taskral favored and gave them away besides, the elders decided I was more trouble than I was worth.

So I drift, and there is always need for a man who knows horseflesh and how to acquire it quietly. The tribes are mustering and good mounts will be worth their weight in silver soon. I would rather break and tend them than steal them, if the work is honest enough.
A man who knows horses is worth keeping close.
A thief is a thief, however freely he gives it away.
Trust me with your horses and your road, and neither will let you down.
A free-handed horse-thief of clan Selarkes, more at home in the saddle than the law.
I deal in what men would rather keep hidden. You are certain you want to hear my trade?

I was eyes and ears for the lords of clan Uzharês, master of the scouts and the whisperers who watch the steppe forts. I knew which captains took bribes, which oaths were rotten, and which fortress would open its gates before a single arrow flew.

Knowledge is a blade with two edges. When the clan's lords fell to feuding over the Taskral's favor, I knew too much of all of them to be allowed to live in peace. The losing side named me traitor; the winning side simply wanted me gone before I sold what I knew.

Now I sell it to whoever pays, and there is no shortage of buyers with a war brewing. Give me a fortress to study and I will tell you how it falls. The Dark Lord's muster has every petty lord watching his neighbor, and a watcher is never out of work.
Eyes inside the enemy's walls win wars cheaply.
A spy who betrayed his own lords will betray me as readily.
Point me at what you must know, and I will bring it back before your enemy knows I looked.
A cast-out scout-master of clan Uzharês, trading the steppe's secrets for silver.
They still tell tales of me at the gathering-grounds, or so I like to think. Here is the truth behind the tales.

I was the champion of the riding-games of clan Alâranin: the spear-casts, the mounted duels, the contests of nerve the nine tribes hold when they gather. For six summers no rider unseated me, and the Taskral's own captains wagered fortunes on my lance.

Champions make enemies, and I made mine by keeping every coin I won and lending none of it. When a rival accused me of a foul cast to break my run, the elders sided with the man who shared his winnings more freely. Pride would not let me stay and be doubted.

So I carry my lance to where it is paid for honestly. The war the Taskral is raising will need men who do not break, and I have never broken at anything. Let others fight for a cause. I fight to be the best, and to be paid like it.
A proven champion's nerve holds when others fail.
A man who hoards his winnings will not spend himself for me.
Wager your battle on my lance and I will not lose you the bet.
A games-champion of clan Alâranin, selling his unbeaten lance to the highest bidder.
An old rider has time for talk, and little else left to him. Sit with me a while.

For thirty years I was lawspeaker to clan Banûgand, the one who remembered the oaths, judged the feuds, and spoke the old words at the gatherings. The young came to me to settle their quarrels before steel did, and mostly they listened.

But a blood-feud is older than any lawspeaker, and when it took my own house I could not judge it cold. I ruled against my kin to keep the peace, and my kin never forgave it. An elder without the trust of his clan is only an old man, so I gave up my seat and my hearth.

Now I offer my counsel to younger captains with wisdom enough to want it. The tribes ride to the Dark Lord's war full of fire and short on memory, and someone must remember what oaths and feuds cost. Perhaps that someone can be of use to you.
An old head's counsel is worth more than a young arm.
I need fighters, not an elder past his riding years.
I am too old to win your battles, but I can keep you from losing them foolishly.
A former lawspeaker of clan Banûgand, offering hard-won counsel to those who will hear it.
I am no great warrior, whatever this scar suggests. But you asked, so I will not hide it.

I was a herder's son of clan Acammes, happy enough with my goats and the open sky, until the Taskral's muster came through and took every man who could hold a spear. They put me in the war-host and called me a soldier.

On my first raid we burned a village that had given us no fight: old men, children, all of it, for serving the wrong lord. I had thought we rode to make Shaghâna strong. When I saw what we truly did, I slipped away in the smoke and have not stopped moving since.

I cannot go home; deserters are made examples of. So I look for a captain who fights men who can fight back, and leaves the helpless alone. I know I am green, but I learn fast, and I will not run from an honest battle. Only from a slaughter.
An honest heart can be forged into a fine soldier.
A frightened farm boy who already deserted once? No.
Take a chance on me and I will repay it. I only ask that the cause be one I can stomach.
A conscripted herder of clan Acammes, deserted after a raid he could not bear.
I make it my business to know things, and to know whom to tell. So, what is it worth to you to know me?

I ran goods and men across the steppe borders for clan Shakar: contraband the Taskral taxed too dear, slaves the fortresses wanted quietly, blades to whichever lord paid. I knew every dry wash and hidden well between the tribes and the eastern roads.

A smuggler survives by selling to all sides and trusting none, and eventually all sides notice. When two clans I had played against each other compared their grievances, the steppe grew too small for me. I took the routes in my head and left the rest behind.

Now those routes and that knowing are for hire. With the Dark Lord's war coming, armies will need what I can move and the paths I can find. I do not pretend to fight for anyone but myself, and I have found honesty about that serves me better than oaths.
A man who knows every hidden road is worth his weight.
He plays all sides. I would be only the next one he sells.
Need something moved, found, or fetched unseen? That is my trade, and I am the best at it.
A border smuggler of clan Shakar, selling his hidden roads to whoever pays.
Every House of Âbanissa is built on its ledgers as much as its spears. I kept one such ledger. Listen.

I was steward and tax-master to the House of Phaxsharân, one of the great stone dynasties of the southern jungles. The tribute of a dozen villages, the upkeep of the war-beasts, the pay of the House spears, all of it passed through my reckoning, and the House prospered for it.

A steward who serves too well learns where his masters cheat the Châjaphân's levy, and a steward who knows too much is dangerous when the House falls from favor. When a rival dynasty whispered against us at court, I was the first they cut loose, to prove the House had nothing to hide.

So I carry my reckoning elsewhere. A war-band is only a small House, and it runs on the same arithmetic: coin in, coin out, and no waste. The Dark Lord's war will ruin the careless and enrich the precise. I intend to be precise, and to serve someone who values it.
A sharp steward keeps an army fed and paid. Useful.
A House man who serves whoever pays is cold comfort.
Set me over your stores and your accounts, and you will campaign longer on less.
A cast-off tax-master of the House of Phaxsharân, selling his ledger-craft to a new master.
I have tended the dying of great Houses. One learns patience, and the worth of plain speech. Ask what you will.

I was physician to the House of Hoshêdharma, trained in the jungle dynasties' old art of medicine: the fevers of the wetlands, the wounds of beast and blade, the slow poisons the Houses favor against one another. For twenty years I kept the dynasty's blood alive.

A physician who knows which lord was poisoned, and by whom, holds secrets no House can leave wandering. When my patron died of a sickness I could not prove was natural, his heir wanted no man alive who might have guessed the truth. I was given a purse and a night to be gone.

Now I tend whoever needs tending and keep a civil tongue. The Châjaphân musters the Houses for the Dark Lord, and war breeds fever and rot as surely as wounds. An army that survives its sicknesses outlasts one that does not. I would see yours outlast its enemies.
A skilled physician is worth a company of spears.
A man who fled a poisoning may have brewed it.
Keep me near your sick and wounded, and fewer of them will go into the ground.
A House physician of Hoshêdharma, who fled rather than share a poisoner's secret.
Stone outlasts the men who raise it. I have raised a great deal of it. Sit, if you would hear how.

I was master-builder to the House of Vasnârad, raising the stone fortresses that crown the jungles of Âbanissa: walls to break an army, gates no ram could split, cisterns to outlast any siege. The Châjaphân's own strongholds bear my hand.

A man who knows how a fortress is built knows exactly how it falls, and rival Houses pay dearly for such knowledge. When mine was found to have sold the weak point of a wall, though I will not say I did, the House could not be seen to keep me. Better an old builder exiled than a dynasty disgraced.

So my craft is for hire, on either side of a wall. With the Dark Lord's war coming, every lord will want his strongholds sound and his enemy's breached. I am too old to climb the ladders, but I can tell you precisely where to set them. Or where to fear them set against you.
A siege-master turns months of war into days.
A builder who sold one wall's secret will sell another's.
Give me your sieges to plan, and walls will cease to be your problem.
An exiled siege-builder of the House of Vasnârad, selling the craft of walls and their breaking.
Discipline, they say, is the soul of an Âbanissan host. I had rather too much of it for my masters' taste. Here is the tale.

I was a captain of spears for the House of Gorazehan, drilling the dynasty's foot into the disciplined ranks that make our hosts feared. My companies held the line where lesser men broke, and I was proud of every one of them.

After a battle, the House lord ordered the captured enemy spears put to death rather than ransomed, a waste, and beneath a soldier. I held that a beaten foe who yields is owed his life, and I said so to the lord's face before my men. Discipline, it seems, is only prized when it does not question.

So I drill other men's companies now, and choose lords who fight like soldiers rather than butchers. The Dark Lord's war will be no gentle thing, I know. But there is a difference between a hard war and a foul one, and I will only lend my craft to the former.
A disciplined captain is the backbone of any host.
An officer who defies his lord will defy me too.
Give me your raw men and a season, and I will give you back soldiers.
A House captain of Gorazehan, cast out for sparing prisoners his lord would have slain.
I am more at home with old scrolls than with swords, but every life turns. Hear mine, if it interests you.

I was a scribe and lore-keeper in the temple-archives of the House of Azadafrozan, copying the dynasty's histories, its treaties, its rolls of the dead. I know the lineages of every great House of Âbanissa and the old tongues the priests no longer speak.

I was too free with what I knew. A petitioner came begging the lineage that would prove his claim against a powerful House, and I gave it freely, as I would to anyone, it was only the truth. The House he challenged did not see it so, and the temple could not protect a scribe who had made such an enemy.

So my learning travels with me now. A captain who can read a captured order, parse a treaty, or know an enemy lord's blood-claims has an edge over one who cannot. The Dark Lord's war is fought with words and lineages as much as spears, and I can fight on that ground at least.
A lettered man is rare and quietly invaluable.
A temple clerk is little use in a hard fight.
I cannot match a soldier's arm, but I can read your enemy better than any of them.
A temple scribe of the House of Azadafrozan, exiled for giving away one truth too freely.
I can be whoever a moment requires. Just now, I am a man telling you the truth, which is rarer for me than you would think.

I was an agent of the House of Artaxshâsan, the kind a dynasty does not admit to keeping. Forged writs, false seals, a letter in any lord's hand you cared to name, I made the documents that won lawsuits, ruined rivals, and shifted the Châjaphân's favor without a blade ever being drawn.

A forger's whole life is one good seal away from the executioner. Mine came when a rival House caught a writ I had made and traced the hand to me. My own masters disowned the work the instant it was dangerous, and I had a single night to vanish before the questioners came.

So my talents are on the market, for those with the stomach to use them. In war, a forged order in the right hands is worth a thousand spears in the wrong place. I do not pretend my trade is honest, but it is effective, and the Dark Lord's war will have ample need of it.
A forger's cunning can win a war without a battle.
A man whose whole craft is lies will lie to me first.
Need a seal forged, a letter placed, an enemy's order turned against him? I am your man.
A House forger of Artaxshâsan, fled one step ahead of the questioners, selling his cunning.
I have spent more years among the great beasts than among men, and trust them further. But I will speak plainly with you.

I was a beast-master of the House of Ardâcheran, keeper of the war-mûmakil, the towering grey beasts of the southern jungles that no enemy line will stand against. I raised them from calves, knew each by name and temper, and walked beneath their feet without fear.

A beast is loyal as no man is, and I came to value that loyalty too highly for my masters. When the House drove a tusker to its death in a reckless charge for a lord's glory, and meant to do the same to the rest, I would not lead them to slaughter. A handler who will not spend his beasts is no use to a House that sees them only as engines.

So I left the beasts I loved rather than watch them die for nothing, and that grief rides with me still. I know warfare and I know command, but I have no taste for throwing lives, beast or man, away for show. Give me a captain who spends his strength wisely, and I will serve him well.
A beast-master's eye for command is a rare thing indeed.
A handler with no beasts is just an old soldier now.
I have no mûmak to bring you, but I bring the judgment that kept them alive. Use it.
A war-beast handler of the House of Ardâcheran, who left rather than lead his beasts to slaughter.
I have made fortunes and lost them, and learned to laugh at both. Pull up a seat for the telling.

I was master of trade for the House of Tîrdahanâ, a merchant-soldier who kept the dynasty's spears fed, armed, and paid through every campaign. Caravans across the jungle roads, contracts with the coast Houses, the gold that turns a rabble into an army, that was my work, and I was generous in it.

I backed the wrong claimant. When the House split over which heir should rule, I poured my fortune into the one I judged the better man. He lost. The victor remembered every coin I had spent against him, and a ruined merchant who chose the losing side is welcome in no House of Âbanissa.

So I rebuild, the only way I know, by making myself useful to someone with a war to fund. The Dark Lord's muster will bankrupt the foolish and enrich the shrewd, and I have learned, expensively, how to tell them apart. Let me keep your army in the field, and I will keep myself in coin.
A merchant who can supply an army is gold itself.
A man who gambled away one fortune may gamble mine.
Trust me with your supply and your trade, and your army will never want for the want of silver.
A ruined trade-master of the House of Tîrdahanâ, rebuilding by provisioning other men's wars.
The jungle hides everything and forgives nothing. I learned to move through it unseen. Listen, and I will tell you how.

I was a pathfinder for the lesser House of Phaxim, scouting the trackless southern jungles where a wrong turn means a slow death. I could read the wet ground, find the dry path through a swamp, and lead a column where the maps showed only green. The Houses paid well for a man who never lost his way.

Knowledge of the secret ways is a jealous thing, and my House guarded its routes closely. When I was caught selling a path to a rival, a small thing I thought, and the coin was good, they branded me faithless and turned me out into the very jungle I had mastered. I survived it. Few would have.

Now my pathfinding is for any captain who needs to go where his enemy does not expect him. War is won by the army that arrives first and unlooked-for, and I can put yours there. The Dark Lord's hosts will march through country that swallows the unprepared. I would see you among the prepared.
A scout who never loses his way is worth an army's eyes.
A pathfinder who sold his own House's routes is a risk.
Send me ahead and your army will never march blind or stray off its road.
A jungle pathfinder of House Phaxim, exiled for selling a secret route, now scouting for hire.
Mine is a short tale and a plain one. I have not lived long enough for a tangled one. Hear it.

I stood in the household guard of the House of Vashan, sworn to the dynasty's hall and the safety of its lord. It was an honest post for an honest man: to stand watch, to guard the gates, to be the last line between my lord and a blade in the dark.

My lord was murdered anyway, by his own brother's hand, while I guarded a gate that was never the danger. I would have named the killer before the Châjaphân's court, but the brother sat the high seat now, and a guardsman's word weighs nothing against a House lord's. To stay was to swear loyalty to the man who killed my master. I would not.

So I carry my sword to where loyalty still means something. I am young, I know, and I have seen one hard year where older men have seen twenty. But I keep my word past breaking, and a captain who can trust the man at his back has something many lords would envy. I would be that man for you.
Unshakable loyalty in a young sword. I will take it.
A guardsman who failed his last lord may fail me.
Give me a post and a lord worth guarding, and I will hold it to the last.
A young household guardsman of House Vashan, who left rather than serve his master's murderer.
